analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling in the North, Mid-, and South Atlantic.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee for the remainder of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would write a permanent ban into law against any new federal leasing for oil, gas, or mineral drilling in three Atlantic planning areas — the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, and South Atlantic. It would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Interior Secretary could not issue a lease or any drilling authorization in those waters. The bill never advanced past committee referral, so no ban was enacted.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic seaboard — tourism businesses, beach towns, and commercial and recreational fishing interests — would benefit from keeping drilling rigs and their associated spill risks out of Atlantic waters. Coastal residents would avoid the pollution and industrialization of their shoreline that offshore drilling can bring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal towns, tourism, and fishing

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or other minerals in the Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, or North Atlantic planning areas.
The ban would be permanent and written directly into statute, so it would apply regardless of which administration set future offshore leasing plans.

The bill's stated purpose is to protect the ocean and coastal economy — its title is the Clean Ocean and Safe Tourism Anti-Drilling Act — aimed at keeping drilling off beaches and fishing grounds that anchor Atlantic coastal economies.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential Atlantic reserves, and workers in the offshore drilling industry would forgo any jobs those leases might have created. The federal treasury would forgo royalty revenue from any production that might have occurred there.

drawbacks.text: The ban permanently forecloses Atlantic energy development: any oil and gas that might exist there could never be produced, forgoing potential domestic supply, industry jobs, and federal royalty revenue.

Because the prohibition applies to 'any other mineral' as well as oil and gas, the ban sweeps broadly, ruling out even future energy or mineral technologies in those waters rather than targeting only the risks of conventional drilling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is regional and asymmetric: Atlantic coastal economies and environments would gain permanent protection from drilling and spill risk, while the nation forgoes energy production and revenue whose actual value is unknown because Atlantic reserves have never been fully assessed. For the coastal states whose beaches and fisheries would bear the risk, the protection is the larger prize; for the oil industry and taxpayers hoping for royalties, the bill is a pure loss. That the bill never got a vote means no actual tradeoff was ever weighed publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act on April 22, 2015, joined by 14 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on May 26, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
Thirty House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republicans signed on.
No further action was taken: the bill remained in subcommittee and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without any vote in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off: no statutory ban was enacted, so Atlantic waters remain legally open to future leasing decisions. Atlantic coastal protection advocates gained nothing from the 114th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests kept the Atlantic legally open

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the Republican majority controlled the Natural Resources Committee and the floor calendar, and the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill permanently bars the industry from leasing or drilling in three Atlantic planning areas, closing off potential reserves, jobs, and production. The costs of drilling — spill risk and coastal industrialization — would fall on coastal residents rather than the companies deciding whether to drill.
Keeping rigs, seismic surveys, and spill risk out of Atlantic waters protects the beaches that drive coastal tourism economies; the bill's title names tourism protection explicitly.
Drilling activity and spills threaten fisheries and fishing grounds; a statutory ban removes that threat from the North, Mid-, and South Atlantic.
The ban forecloses potential federal royalty revenue and domestic energy supply from Atlantic waters, though no proven reserves there were on the table at the time.
